facts.claim: The number of bacteria in the body is of the same order as the number of human cells.
facts.quote: Our analysis also updates the widely-cited 10:1 ratio, showing that the number of bacteria in the body is actually of the same order as the number of human cells

facts.claim: The number of bacteria in a 70 kg man is estimated to be 3.8·1013.
facts.quote: We estimate the total number of bacteria in the 70 kg "reference man" to be 3.8·1013.

facts.claim: The total mass of bacteria in the body is about 0.2 kg.
facts.quote: and their total mass is about 0.2 kg.

facts.claim: The number of human cells in the body is revised to 3.0·1013.
facts.quote: For human cells, we identify the dominant role of the hematopoietic lineage to the total count (≈90%) and revise past estimates to 3.0·1013 human cells.

facts.claim: The total body counts are estimated at ≈36 trillion cells in the male, ≈28 trillion in the female, and ≈17 trillion in the child.
facts.quote: In total, we estimate total body counts of ≈36 trillion cells in the male, ≈28 trillion in the female, and ≈17 trillion in the child.

research.angle: While the 10:1 ratio is widely cited, research shows the number of bacteria in the body is actually of the same order as the number of human cells.
research.verdict: The evidence shows that bacterial cell counts are roughly comparable to human cell counts, contradicting the common 10:1 ratio.
research.caveat: The bacterial count is based on a 70 kg "reference man" and does not account for individual variation.
